records.answer: Agent ID does not route or meter model calls. The Global Secure Access agent page lists forwarded traffic types as HTTP nodes, custom connectors and MCP server connectors, not model traffic.
records.gaps: No per-agent model routing, quota or cost enforcement.
records.options: Use an AI gateway such as Azure API Management in front of model endpoints.

records.answer: Global Secure Access can proxy Copilot Studio agent traffic from HTTP nodes, custom connectors and MCP server connectors and apply web content filtering, threat intelligence filtering and network file filtering. Conditional Access controls token issuance to MCP servers and APIs per agent identity or blueprint. Microsoft also describes prompt injection detection at the network layer.
records.gaps: Network forwarding is documented only for Copilot Studio agents and applies tenant-wide through the baseline profile, not per agent. No tool schema validation or per-tool rate limits. Requires Agent 365 licensing.
records.options: Enable traffic forwarding per Power Platform environment and test filtering against a known blocked category. Use an MCP gateway for schema and rate controls.

records.answer: Conditional Access can block an agent identity from obtaining tokens for a data resource such as SharePoint, and Global Secure Access network file filtering can restrict file uploads and downloads in Copilot Studio agent traffic. There is no content-level DLP in Agent ID.
records.gaps: No retrieval-level filtering or sensitivity-aware DLP. Controls act at token issuance or network file type.
records.options: Pair with Microsoft Purview DLP and sensitivity labels for content controls.

records.answer: Because a callee agent can be an Entra-protected resource, Conditional Access policies scoped by agent identity, blueprint or custom security attribute decide which agents get tokens for it. Risk policies can block risky agents from reaching other agents.
records.gaps: Enforcement is at token issuance, not on the message path. No A2A message schema checks.
records.options: Model allowed agent pairs as app role assignments on each callee and test denial with an unassigned caller.

records.answer: Agent ID has no feature for human review of agent output.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use the agent platform's review tools.

records.answer: ID Protection detects anomalous agent identity behaviour such as sign-in spikes, unfamiliar resource access, failed access attempts, directory reconnaissance and early-life malicious activity. Learning Mode suppresses behavioural alerts for agents with little history.
records.gaps: Detections are offline and based on identity and access signals, not task output. In OBO flows risk is attributed to the user, not the agent. Licensing is moving to Agent 365.
records.options: Combine with runtime monitoring of agent actions and outputs.

records.answer: Agent ID does not report token, infrastructure or labour costs.

records.options: Use cost tooling on the model and hosting platforms.

records.answer: Agent ID does not monitor load or infrastructure performance.
records.gaps: Outside product category.

records.answer: Admins can see API permissions, roles and group memberships held by each agent identity in the Entra admin center. Copilot Studio attaches each configured connector as an API permission on the agent identity so admins can see what an agent can call.
records.gaps: No graph or map view of agent network reach was found. Non-Entra access such as API keys is not visible.
records.options: Export permissions through Microsoft Graph and build a reach view.

records.answer: Entra audit logs record agent identity creation, updates and deletion with agentType and blueprintId on initiator, performer and target. Sign-in logs record each agent token acquisition and can be filtered by agent type.
records.gaps: Logs cover identity operations and sign-ins only, not agent inputs, outputs or reasoning. Tamper resistance is not documented. Some agent fields need the Graph beta endpoint.
records.options: Export logs to immutable storage through diagnostic settings and capture action content in the agent platform.

records.answer: ID Protection produces agent risk detections, a Risky Agents report and Graph collections riskyAgents and agentRiskDetections, exportable to Log Analytics, event hubs or a SIEM. Responders can confirm compromise, which triggers risk-based blocking, or disable the agent. Sponsors are shown on risky agent details.
records.gaps: Session correlation and redaction are not described. Risk detections are retained 90 days. Detections are offline.
records.options: Stream sign-in, audit and risk logs to Microsoft Sentinel and map sponsors to response ownership.

records.answer: Agent ID does not inspect model files or record model lineage.

records.options: Use a model scanning tool.

records.answer: Agent ID does not run adversarial tests.

records.answer: Entra and Microsoft Graph hold an inventory of blueprints, agent identities and agents' user accounts with descriptions, publisher and sponsors. records.gaps: Covers agent identities only, not models or tools. The comprehensive registry is Agent 365.
records.options: Register blueprints in the Agent 365 registry and query Graph for identity records.

records.answer: Blueprints declare required resource access that admins review at consent, and permissions require admin or user consent. Access packages route agent access requests through configured approvers.
records.gaps: No documented approval gate for creating an agent identity itself. Covers access, not models or tools.
records.options: Restrict Agent ID Developer role and require a production handshake review, as Microsoft best practice suggests.

records.answer: The ID Protection dashboard summarises risky agents by risk level, and the Risky Agents report lists flagged agents with sponsors.

records.answer: Multitenant blueprints from external publishers carry a verified publisher and are added or removed by creating or deleting the blueprint principal. Third-party agents on AWS Bedrock or n8n can be given Entra identities and governed the same way.
records.gaps: No periodic reassessment workflow for external agents or tools beyond access reviews.
records.options: Include external blueprints in access reviews and review verified publisher status.

records.answer: Registering an agent creates a workload principal record in Universal Directory alongside human identities, with owners, credentials and an optional linked OIDC app. Custom agents are registered manually and builder platform agents are imported. The Agent Gateway attributes tool calls to the agent's workload principal regardless of credential rotation.
records.gaps: No documented link from the agent record to a runtime, build or release version.
records.options: Record runtime and release in agent description or custom attributes, and test that imported agents keep a stable record across platform re-syncs.

records.answer: Agent Gateway obtains downstream OAuth tokens by STS token exchange and injects them, so the agent never holds tool credentials. Resource connections can hand out secrets and service accounts vaulted in Okta Privileged Access by resource indicator. Auth0 Token Vault stores connected account tokens and refreshes and exchanges them without user action.
records.gaps: Revoked agent tokens stay valid at the gateway until expiry. Rotation of vaulted secrets and Token Vault encryption are not described on the pages read. The gateway only supports upstreams that accept OAuth bearer tokens.
records.options: Set short token lifetimes, test revocation latency end to end, and use Okta Privileged Access rotation for static secrets.

records.answer: Cross App Access issues a short-lived ID-JAG carrying the user's identity, which the resource authorisation server exchanges for its own access token under admin policy set in Okta. Agent Gateway exchanges the agent token for downstream tokens on behalf of the user, with first-use consent and stored per-user refresh tokens. A linked app restricts an agent to acting for users currently signed in to that app.
records.gaps: Downstream apps must implement the ID-JAG grant. Delegation chains beyond one hop are not described.
records.options: Check which target apps support XAA in the Okta Integration Network and test multi-hop delegation explicitly.

records.answer: The Connect to another AI agent resource connection lets one agent call another under the target's identity through an Okta authorisation server and audience, with allowed scopes. Okta announced Agent-to-Agent Connections as GA at Oktane 2026, with rules on which agents can call others and an auditable handoff chain.
records.gaps: Cross-organisation trust boundaries and A2A protocol support are not described.
records.options: Test a two-agent chain and confirm the System Log shows both identities.

records.answer: Okta controls access to remote resources by token. The pages read describe no control over what an agent can do on its local host, such as file or shell access.
records.gaps: Local host permissions sit outside the product.
records.options: Use endpoint or harness controls. ISPM endpoint discovery only inventories local agents.

records.answer: Resource connections bind an agent to authorisation servers, apps, MCP servers, secrets, service accounts or other agents, with scopes set to allow all, only allow or disallow. Deactivating a connection denies all further access requests to that resource. Agent Gateway exposes only admin-selected tools per virtual MCP server.
records.gaps: Per-tool authorisation rules beyond exposure and argument level constraints are not described.
records.options: Combine scope limits with downstream app authorisation and test that unexposed tools are absent from tools/list.

records.answer: Auth0 for AI Agents offers asynchronous authorisation with CIBA and RAR, so an agent waits for a user to approve an action on a separate device, with Guardian push showing authorisation details. In Okta workforce, approval routing applies to access requests for agent-linked apps, not to individual agent actions.
records.gaps: CIBA needs an Auth0 Enterprise plan or add-on. Binding message, expiry and replay handling are not described on the page read. No per-action approval in the Okta workforce agent product.
records.options: Use Auth0 CIBA with RAR for high-risk actions and test denial and replay behaviour.

records.answer: Admins register or import agents, add owners and credentials, and create, edit, deactivate or remove resource connections. Agents can be deactivated, and the kill switch combines deactivating the agent, its linked app and its authorisation server.
records.gaps: Kill switch is manual and existing tokens remain valid until expiry. Runtime revocation at the gateway is planned for Q4.
records.options: Script deactivation and token revocation through the Okta API and test time to full cut-off.

records.answer: Flagged agent actions can be routed for human review by CORIE, and policy violations are routed to owners through workflows. There is no documented queue for human review of model output content before release.

records.options: Use the application's review step and record outcomes in OneTrust as evidence.

records.answer: The runtime controls page describes monitoring of model and agent behaviour, evaluation metrics for quality, safety issue detection and guardrail effectiveness tracking. The AI Policy Engine can flag drift in third-party models.
records.gaps: Which evaluation methods and anomaly detection techniques are used, and which platforms supply the signals, is not documented.
records.options: Confirm which integrations supply evaluation and drift signals and test with a known drifted model.

records.answer: The AI governance page says it tracks usage and token-consumption signals where supported. No cost, savings or yield reporting is documented.
records.gaps: No cost attribution, labour savings or profit metrics.
records.options: Use FinOps or gateway cost tooling for spend and yield.

records.answer: OneTrust does not monitor infrastructure load or performance for AI workloads. AI Guard publishes its own service metrics, which concern the OneTrust component only.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use the cloud provider or observability platform.

records.answer: The platform maps relationships and dependencies across the AI estate, linking agents to models, data and integrations, and the CORIE Trust Graph maps AI systems to enterprise data, vendors and identities.
records.gaps: No documented view of each agent's live network reach or effective permissions against downstream systems.
records.options: Check in a demo whether the dependency map reflects actual tool and data permissions or only declared metadata.

records.answer: CORIE records the agent, request, purpose, outcome and governing policy for each decision, and the Evidence Ledger records what was considered, which control applied and what action was taken. The governance FAQ describes a continuous audit trail from intake through monitoring.
records.gaps: Tamper resistance is not documented. Model inputs, outputs and reasoning are not captured, and AI Guard states it does not collect prompts or responses.
records.options: Request details of Evidence Ledger integrity controls and export, and pair with a gateway log for full input and output capture.

records.answer: The runtime controls page describes detecting sensitive data exposure and policy violations through log analysis and routing violations to owners. No SIEM export, session correlation or redaction for security telemetry was found. AI Guard has a metrics exporters page that was not opened.
records.gaps: SIEM integration and actor correlation are not established from the pages checked.
records.options: Read the AI Guard metrics exporter documentation and ask OneTrust about SIEM connectors for violation events.

records.answer: Inventory records capture model type, data sources, lineage and lifecycle changes, and templates support EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001 assessments. Model file inspection and AI BoM generation are not documented.
records.gaps: No model file scanning, signature checks or machine-readable AI BoM.
records.options: Use a model scanning tool and attach its output to the OneTrust record as evidence.

records.answer: OneTrust does not assess or harden inference or tool execution containers, harnesses or hosts.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use container and host security tooling.

records.answer: No SBOM generation, scanning or code review of MCP servers, CLIs, skills or extensions is documented. MCP policy enforcement governs invocation, not the assurance of the tool itself.
records.gaps: Outside the documented scope.
records.options: Use software composition analysis and MCP scanning tools and record results in the registry.

records.answer: No scanning of third-party MCP registries, plugins or skills for squatting, metadata poisoning or compromise is documented.
records.gaps: Outside the documented scope.
records.options: Use a dedicated MCP or package supply chain scanner.

records.answer: Datasets are inventoried alongside models and agents with ownership and lineage, and Databricks Unity Catalog is a named integration. AI Guard uses OneTrust's Data Discovery classification engine.
records.gaps: No documented sanitisation of training or feature data or infrastructure controls for feature stores.
records.options: Combine with data platform governance and confirm what the Unity Catalog integration ingests.

records.answer: The registry page describes shadow AI identification by comparing intake, procurement, vendor reviews, attestations, integrations and API usage, flagging unknown systems and routing them to review. Agent detection discovers agents across Amazon Bedrock, Azure Foundry and Google Vertex.
records.gaps: Discovery of employee use of public AI tools depends on connected sources. Connector coverage for SaaS and endpoints is not listed.
records.options: Confirm connector list and test discovery of an undeclared agent in a connected cloud account.

records.answer: No automated adversarial testing or red teaming is documented. The AI governance page surfaces evaluation metrics and links to guidance only.
records.gaps: Outside the documented scope.
records.options: Use an AI red teaming tool and attach results as assessment evidence.

records.answer: The AI registry is a system of record for use cases, models, agents, datasets, vendors and SaaS with embedded AI, with standardised metadata, version history and deployment status.
records.gaps: Tool schemas and software component records are not mentioned.
records.options: Extend registry fields for tool schemas, or link to an external component inventory.

records.answer: Configurable intake, approval, attestation and signoff workflows route reviews by risk, with approval gates at intake, deployment and material change. Unknown discovered systems are routed into review.
records.gaps: Workflows rely on configuration. Enforcement of approval in the runtime depends on separate controls.
records.options: Configure intake forms per asset type and test that an unapproved agent is flagged at runtime.

records.answer: The AI Program Center reports runtime risk and control performance and tracks blocked, redacted, routed and allowed activity by system, model, agent or application. The Governance Command Center, announced September 2026, shows risk posture, decisions and exceptions.
records.gaps: Governance Command Center availability is not stated. Posture Management for Regulations is in private preview.
records.options: Validate dashboard coverage against the control set in a pilot.

records.answer: AI Policy Manager defines acceptable use and required controls, with a policy library of prebuilt standards-aligned policies, custom policies and versioned policy tracking including applicability and exceptions.
records.gaps: Review cadence and publication mechanics are not detailed.
records.options: Test policy versioning and review reminders in a pilot.

records.answer: Registry records carry lifecycle states of proposed, in development, in testing, approved for production, restricted, under reassessment and retired, linked to approvals, assessments and monitoring.
records.gaps: Lifecycle state is a governance record. It does not move the asset in the runtime.
records.options: Integrate lifecycle state with deployment pipelines.

records.answer: Each registry record shows the accountable owner, and the solution page assigns ownership and lifecycle status across systems, models, agents, datasets and vendors, with control ownership shown.
records.gaps: Ownership of individual decisions made by agents is not described beyond CORIE logging.
records.options: Require owner fields at intake and test reassignment on staff changes.

records.answer: Risk is evaluated consistently across homegrown and third-party AI, tiered automatically and revalidated after material change, using templates for the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001. Risk and control recommendations are due to be generally available in winter.
records.gaps: EU AI Act page does not show how prohibited or high-risk categories are determined.
records.options: Run sample use cases through the EU AI Act template and check classification output.

records.answer: Record-level change history captures prompt updates, model swaps, retrieval source changes and new agent actions, with who approved them and whether reassessment is required. OneTrust does not version, release or roll back the artefacts themselves.
records.gaps: Release and rollback happen in other systems. Detection of changes depends on discovery and integrations.
records.options: Link CI/CD release events to OneTrust records and test reassessment triggers.

records.answer: The solution page tracks policy exceptions and remediation status alongside control ownership and policy history, and the Governance Command Center shows exceptions.
records.gaps: Exception approval, expiry and periodic review and formal risk acceptance are not described.
records.options: Configure an exception workflow with expiry dates and test reminders.

records.answer: The AI governance pages checked do not address retention, deletion or residency for AI inputs, outputs or agent memory. OneTrust privacy products may cover data retention generally, but they were outside this research scope.
records.gaps: Whether OneTrust privacy and data governance modules apply to AI inputs and memory is untested.
records.options: Check OneTrust data retention and privacy modules for AI data stores.

records.answer: The platform generates audit-ready evidence from assessments and approvals, with a continuous audit trail from intake through monitoring. The EU AI Act page describes audit trails created as governance actions occur and post-market monitoring with recorded corrective actions.
records.gaps: Evidence export formats and mapping to control IDs are not detailed.
records.options: Test evidence export against an ISO 42001 control set.

records.answer: Third-party AI is assessed in AI Governance and vendors are tracked in the inventory. The Third-Party Management module provides intake, tiering, auto-approval for low risk, assessments, event-triggered automation and continuous monitoring through RiskRecon, SecurityScorecard and HackNotice.
records.gaps: Scheduled periodic reassessment and vendor retirement are not described specifically. Third-Party Management is a separate module.
records.options: Configure reassessment schedules and offboarding workflows and test them for an AI vendor.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not issue or manage agent or workload identities. It tests agents as targets. Checked the enterprise overview and the teams page, which cover Promptfoo users, teams and service account API keys only.
records.gaps: No agent identity linked to owner, runtime or release.
records.options: Use an identity platform or agent registry for agent IDs.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not broker credentials to agents. Service accounts issue API keys for Promptfoo itself, for example for CI/CD. Tracing masks credential-like attributes in displayed traces, which is test hygiene rather than brokerage.
records.gaps: No scoped delivery, rotation or revocation of agent credentials.
records.options: Use a secrets manager or credential broker. Promptfoo red team plugins can test whether secrets leak into model output.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not propagate user identity to downstream services. Its bola, bfla and rbac plugins test whether a target enforces delegated authority, which is covered under c7-10.
records.gaps: No on-behalf-of mechanism.
records.options: Implement OBO in the agent platform and test it with the bola and bfla plugins.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not secure agent-to-agent traffic. Its A2A provider connects to an A2A agent as a test target with bearer, basic, API key or OAuth 2.0 auth, and only the HTTP+JSON binding is supported.
records.gaps: No authentication or authorisation between production agents.
records.options: Use an A2A-capable gateway or identity layer. Use the A2A provider to red team A2A agents.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not constrain actions an agent can take on its local host. The shell-injection plugin tests whether a target can be driven to run commands.
records.gaps: No local scope enforcement.
records.options: Use the agent runtime or sandbox for local scopes and test them with the shell-injection and excessive-agency plugins.

records.answer: The MCP Proxy product page says administrators can give specific users and applications access to specific MCP servers, limited to the tools and data they need. Other connected systems are not covered, and the detail comes from a product page rather than configuration docs.
records.gaps: Only MCP traffic. No documented policy syntax or per-action scope model.
records.options: Request MCP Proxy configuration docs and test scope bypass with the mcp, bola and bfla plugins.

records.answer: Promptfoo has no runtime approval step bound to a proposed agent action. Checked guardrails, which return allow, log, warn, block or error to the calling app without a human decision.
records.gaps: No human approval workflow.
records.options: Use the agent framework's approval feature.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not provision agents. Enterprise RBAC controls who can create and edit red team targets and configurations, which are test records rather than agent identities.
records.gaps: No agent identity or permission lifecycle.
records.options: Use the agent platform or IAM for provisioning.

records.answer: Promptfoo is a testing tool and does not orchestrate agent workflows.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Not applicable.

records.answer: Promptfoo calls model providers to run evals and does not host inference. Provider ids name an explicit model version and accept settings such as temperature and max_tokens, which pins the model under test only.
records.gaps: No inference service, data handling terms or operating limits.
records.options: Use the model provider's own controls. Promptfoo can compare model versions before release.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not provide an agent execution environment or sandbox.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Not applicable.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not provide agent session memory. The cross-session-leak and pii:session plugins test session isolation in a target.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Test session isolation with those plugins.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not provide a tool-executing harness for production agents.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Not applicable.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not provide persistent agent memory. The agentic:memory-poisoning plugin tests a target's memory.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Test memory with the memory-poisoning plugin.

records.answer: Enterprise guardrails screen INPUT and OUTPUT through a REST evaluate endpoint that returns an allow, log, warn or block action. Policies are generated from successful red team attacks, plus manual policies. The application must call the endpoint itself, and there is no routing, quota or cost enforcement.
records.gaps: Not an inline gateway. Only blocks patterns similar to known vulnerabilities. No per-user quotas.
records.options: Pair with a model gateway for routing and quotas, and call the guardrail endpoint from it.

records.answer: MCP Proxy allowlists approved MCP servers and grants users and apps access to specific servers. Guardrails support TOOL_CALL_INPUT and TOOL_CALL_OUTPUT placements to validate tool arguments and results. Schema enforcement, quotas and internet egress control are not documented.
records.gaps: MCP only. Product page detail. No egress or rate controls described.
records.options: Verify MCP Proxy behaviour in a trial and add an egress proxy for non-MCP tools.

records.answer: Guardrail fast filters can catch sensitive text such as card numbers and SSNs, and a PII filter on TOOL_CALL_INPUT can stop data reaching third-party APIs. MCP Proxy monitors for PII exposure and alerts. No retrieval authorisation is documented.
records.gaps: Regex-level DLP. No per-user retrieval control.
records.options: Use a data gateway or DLP service for retrieval control.

records.answer: Promptfoo has no gateway for agent-to-agent traffic. The A2A provider is a test client only.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use an A2A gateway.

records.answer: In the eval view reviewers can mark individual test results as pass or failure, and can add comments to findings. This reviews test outputs, not production agent output.
records.gaps: No production output review queue.
records.options: Use an observability or HITL tool for production review.

records.answer: Evals and red teams can run in CI/CD to catch regressions as the application changes. Trajectory assertions check tool use, tool arguments, tool sequence and goal success from OpenTelemetry traces. This is test-time validation, not production anomaly detection.
records.gaps: No runtime anomaly detection on live traffic.
records.options: Run scheduled evals against production-like targets and pair with runtime monitoring.

records.answer: The cost assertion checks that a test's cost is below a threshold, and traces record token usage for instrumented providers. Provider config accepts inputCost and outputCost overrides. Cost covers eval runs, not production spend or yield.
records.gaps: No production cost, labour or yield reporting.
records.options: Use a model gateway or FinOps tool for production cost.

records.answer: Promptfoo offers latency assertions and span duration checks for test runs only. It does not monitor infrastructure load or anomalies.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use APM or infrastructure monitoring.

records.answer: The target discovery agent extracts a target's purpose, limitations, tools and user context, and the tool-discovery plugin probes for exposed tools. This gives a test-time view of what an agent can reach, not a maintained map of downstream scopes.
records.gaps: Point-in-time and model-reported. No connectivity graph.
records.options: Combine discovery output with an agent registry or the MCP Proxy server list.

records.answer: Enterprise audit logs record administrative actions on users, teams, roles, permissions and service accounts with actor, target and timestamp, retrievable through GET /api/v1/audit-logs. Eval runs are tracked separately. Tamper protection and retention are not described.
records.gaps: Admin plane only. No agent input, output or reasoning ledger. No integrity guarantee documented.
records.options: Export audit logs to a WORM store or SIEM.

records.answer: Webhooks emit issue.created, issue.updated, issue.status_changed and related events with full issue state, and the docs name SIEM integration as a use. MCP Proxy describes real-time alerts for sensitive data exposure and policy violations. These are vulnerability events, not session-correlated runtime telemetry.
records.gaps: No actor or session correlation of live agent activity documented.
records.options: Forward webhooks to the SIEM and take runtime telemetry from the agent platform.

records.answer: ModelAudit statically scans model files in many formats, including PyTorch, ONNX, SafeTensors, GGUF and pickle, for malicious code, embedded secrets, licence issues and weight anomalies, from local or remote sources such as Hugging Face and S3. The --sbom flag emits a CycloneDX SBOM with licence data. Lineage and compliance attestation are not covered.
records.gaps: No model lineage or signed attestation. Static scan only.
records.options: Pair with model signing and provenance tooling.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not assure inference or tool execution containers and hosts. ModelAudit reads OCI container manifests to find model files, and red team plugins such as shell-injection and ssrf test runtime boundaries from outside, which sit under c7-3 and c7-10.
records.gaps: No host or container hardening checks.
records.options: Use container and host security tooling.

records.answer: Code scanning reviews pull requests for LLM risks such as prompt injection, PII exposure and excessive agency, traced across files, and posts findings to GitHub Code Scanning. The MCP security guide tests an organisation's own MCP servers directly and through an assistant for authorisation, input validation and data leakage.
records.gaps: No SBOM for MCP servers, CLIs or skills. The code scanning page does not mention MCP.
records.options: Add SCA and SBOM tooling for tool packages.

records.answer: The MCP guide and mcp plugin test tool poisoning, tool metadata injection, tool shadowing and rug pulls in multi-server setups. MCP Proxy restricts use to approved servers. There is no registry scanning for squatting or package compromise.
records.gaps: Tests model behaviour against malicious tools, not the packages themselves.
records.options: Use a package or registry scanner alongside these tests.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not govern data or feature stores. The rag-poisoning plugin tests whether poisoned documents affect a target, under c7-10.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use data governance tooling.

records.answer: No shadow AI discovery is documented. Target discovery profiles a system already chosen for testing, and the MCP Proxy page does not describe discovery of unapproved servers.
records.gaps: No discovery of unsanctioned AI use.
records.options: Use a CASB, SaaS discovery or endpoint tool.

records.answer: Promptfoo red teaming sends generated adversarial inputs to models, RAG pipelines, agents and MCP or A2A targets and grades the responses. Plugins cover bola, bfla, rbac, ssrf, shell and SQL injection, indirect prompt injection, RAG and memory poisoning, data exfiltration and MCP attacks. Runs can be one-off or in CI/CD, and red team tracing feeds application traces back into attacks.
records.gaps: Black-box focus. Token cost can be high for some strategies. Coverage limited to configured plugins.
records.options: Write the purpose field and custom policies carefully and run on each release.

records.answer: Promptfoo Enterprise keeps a list of red team targets per team, which is test configuration rather than an inventory of models, agents and tools. ModelAudit SBOMs cover individual model files.
records.gaps: No asset registry.
records.options: Use an AI asset registry and feed it ModelAudit SBOMs.

records.answer: No submission or approval workflow for models, agents or tools is documented. MCP Proxy enforces an allowlist of approved servers but does not describe how servers are submitted or approved.
records.gaps: No registration workflow.
records.options: Use a governance platform for approval, and test candidates with Promptfoo before approval.

records.answer: Enterprise findings list vulnerabilities by target, severity, status, risk category and type, and reports show the most successful strategies and most critical issues. Reports can be filtered by framework, including OWASP LLM, NIST AI RMF and MITRE ATLAS. Posture covers red team results only.
records.gaps: No view of control coverage beyond testing.
records.options: Feed findings into a GRC posture tool through the API or webhooks.

records.answer: Custom policies can be defined in red team config with the policy plugin, and guardrails keep manual policies alongside generated ones. These are testable rules, with no documented ownership, publication or review cycle.
records.gaps: No AI policy lifecycle.
records.options: Hold policies in a GRC tool and express testable rules as Promptfoo custom policies in version control.

records.answer: Promptfoo supports the testing stage of the lifecycle and recommends checkpoints for model testing, pre-deployment, CI/CD and post-deployment monitoring. It does not track proposal, production state or retirement.
records.gaps: Only a test gate.
records.options: Use Promptfoo results as a stage gate in a lifecycle tool.

records.answer: Enterprise teams own their targets, configurations and results, but no accountable owner field for agents, models or tools is documented.
records.gaps: No ownership model.
records.options: Record owners in an asset registry.

records.answer: Red team findings carry critical, high, medium or low severity set by plugin and adjustable per plugin or per finding, and grading uses the application context given for the target. Use case risk classification and control selection are not covered.
records.gaps: No use case risk tiering.
records.options: Classify use cases in a GRC tool and map tiers to Promptfoo plugin sets.

records.answer: Evals and red teams can run in CI/CD to catch regressions when prompts, models or tools change. Approval, versioning and rollback are not provided.
records.gaps: Regression testing only.
records.options: Use CI/CD branch protection with Promptfoo as a required check.

records.answer: Findings can be marked Fixed, False Positive or Ignore, with comments for context. No accepted-risk status, approver or expiry is documented.
records.gaps: No formal exception workflow.
records.options: Record exceptions in a GRC tool and link the finding ID.

records.answer: Promptfoo does not govern retention of agent data. Self-hosted instances store evals in SQLite on a mapped volume, and the docs describe no retention or deletion controls.
records.gaps: No retention, residency or deletion controls documented.
records.options: Manage eval data storage through the host and confirm Enterprise terms with the vendor.

records.answer: Red team reports can be filtered by OWASP LLM Top 10, OWASP API Top 10, NIST AI RMF and MITRE ATLAS, and findings export as PDF reports, CSV and SARIF or through the API. Evidence covers adversarial testing only.
records.gaps: No traceability to other control evidence.
records.options: Attach exports to the audit evidence store per release.

records.answer: MCP Proxy allows only approved, vetted MCP servers. Evals can compare external models before adoption. Periodic reassessment and retirement are not documented.
records.gaps: No third-party review cycle.
records.options: Schedule recurring Promptfoo runs against third-party models and tools and track them in a vendor risk tool.

records.answer: The Agent Gateway registers A2A agents with an agent ID, set in the Admin UI, the /v1/agents API or config.yaml. Calls can carry an X-LiteLLM-Agent-Id header for spend attribution, and JWT auth can bind tokens to registered agents. Agent records hold a name, URL, protocol version and agent card fields, but the docs do not describe a linked owner or release record.
records.gaps: No documented owner or release linkage on the agent record. Attribution via X-LiteLLM-Agent-Id is a caller-supplied header. Workload identity for agents that call LiteLLM depends on the virtual key they hold.
records.options: Issue one virtual key per agent with owner metadata, and test whether a key can spoof another agent's X-LiteLLM-Agent-Id header.

records.answer: Clients authenticate with virtual keys while provider and MCP credentials stay in the gateway. Keys can be scoped to models, given a duration, blocked and unblocked, and capped by upperbound parameters. Key regeneration with a grace period, scheduled auto-rotation and secret manager integration (AWS, Azure, Google, HashiCorp Vault, CyberArk) require an Enterprise licence.
records.gaps: Rotation and secret manager storage need an Enterprise licence. Storing virtual keys in a secret manager is off by default. Keeping provider secrets out of model context depends on clients not passing them through.
records.options: Enable rotation_interval and store_virtual_keys under an Enterprise licence, and confirm a blocked or expired key is rejected across all proxy instances.

records.answer: For MCP servers, auth_type oauth2_token_exchange exchanges the caller's bearer token at the identity provider (RFC 8693, or Entra jwt-bearer OBO) and forwards only the scoped token. Tokens are cached per subject token and server, so users get separate tokens. JWT auth can set the end-user ID from a verified claim, which overrides any request value.
records.gaps: The A2A gateway does not automatically forward the caller's virtual key or end-user ID to backend agents. JWT auth needs an Enterprise licence.
records.options: Use OBO for MCP servers that accept identity provider tokens, and test that a request without a subject token is refused rather than falling back to a shared credential.

records.answer: The A2A gateway authenticates callers with a LiteLLM virtual key and checks whether the key and its team may invoke the target agent, returning 403 otherwise. Agents can require a trace ID on inbound calls. The docs do not describe agent-to-agent trust boundaries or mutual authentication between agents.
records.gaps: No rules on which agents may call which other agents. Caller identity is not forwarded to the backend agent.
records.options: Give each calling agent its own key restricted to permitted target agents, and authenticate the gateway to backend agents at the agent runtime.

records.answer: LiteLLM is a network gateway and does not run on or control the agent's local host. Checked the MCP, A2A, guardrail and tool policy docs for local file, process or shell controls and found none.
records.gaps: No control over local host actions.
records.options: Use the agent harness or endpoint sandbox for local scopes.

records.answer: MCP Permission Management assigns allowed servers at key, team, end user, agent, internal user and organisation level, intersecting the lists so the most restrictive wins. allowed_tools, disallowed_tools and allowed_params restrict tools and their parameters, with 403 on violation. A2A agent access and model access are scoped per key and team in the same way.
records.gaps: Servers marked allow_all_keys bypass per-key grants. Keys with an empty list inherit the team list unless require_key_mcp_access_defined is set.
records.options: Set require_key_mcp_access_defined, avoid allow_all_keys for sensitive servers, and test parameter restrictions with crafted tool calls.

records.answer: On the MCP gateway, require_approval controls whether the proxy runs tool calls itself. Unless it is set to never, tool calls are returned to the client for review. The approval decision, its binding to the exact call and replay handling sit with the client application.
records.gaps: No gateway-side approval record, approver identity, denial handling or replay protection is documented.
records.options: Implement approval in the client or harness and log approver identity alongside the LiteLLM call ID.

records.answer: Keys, teams, users, agents, MCP servers and models are created, updated, blocked and deleted through the Admin UI, API or config.yaml. key_generation_settings, upperbound parameters and custom key policy hooks restrict who can create keys and with what limits. Organisation and team admin roles and team member permissions are Premium features under an Enterprise licence.
records.gaps: No approval step for agent creation. Fine-grained RBAC needs an Enterprise licence. Config-defined agents need a restart to change.
records.options: Manage agents and keys through config.yaml or Terraform under change control, and enable audit logs to record changes.

records.answer: LiteLLM does not sequence agent workflows. It retries model calls, falls back across model groups and cools down unhealthy deployments. For agents it caps iterations and spend per session and offers an admin-fired kill switch webhook to stop an agent runtime.
records.gaps: No workflow definition, task delegation or recovery of agent state. Retries apply per model call only.
records.options: Use an orchestration framework for sequencing and rely on LiteLLM for per-call retry and session caps.

records.answer: Each model name maps to explicit provider deployments with API base, credentials and per-deployment rpm limits, managed in config.yaml or the model API. Timeouts, context window pre-call checks and region_name filtering for routing are configurable. LiteLLM routes to providers and does not host model weights.
records.gaps: Data handling at the provider depends on provider terms. Region filtering needs enable_pre_call_checks.
records.options: Pin deployments to provider model versions and regions, and test that fallbacks respect region and access rules (enforce_fallback_model_access).

records.answer: LiteLLM provides no code interpreter or sandboxed host for agents. Checked the proxy, MCP and A2A docs.
records.gaps: Execution environment is out of scope.
records.options: Use a separate sandbox runtime.

records.answer: LiteLLM uses session IDs (x-litellm-trace-id) to count iterations and spend, with counters expiring after an hour. It does not store session state for agents. Checked the A2A and iteration budget docs.
records.gaps: No session memory store, access control or resumption.
records.options: Keep session state in the agent framework.

records.answer: LiteLLM proxies tool calls to MCP servers and can run them when require_approval is never, but it is not an agent harness. Checked the MCP docs.
records.gaps: No harness for local tool execution.
records.options: Use an agent framework or coding agent harness.

records.answer: Spend logs can store prompts and responses when store_prompts_in_spend_logs is on, but this is logging, not agent memory. No long-term memory feature is documented.
records.gaps: No persistent agent memory.
records.options: Use a memory store in the agent framework.

records.answer: Virtual keys enforce allowed models, budgets, TPM, RPM and parallel limits per key, user, team, organisation, agent and customer, with per-model limits. Guardrails run pre_call, during_call and post_call, including built-in prompt injection detection by similarity or LLM check and third-party providers such as Lakera and Bedrock. Per key, team and model guardrail control requires an Enterprise licence.
records.gaps: Budgets need Postgres and fail open without it. Rate limits need Redis to be shared across instances. Several named guardrail integrations need an Enterprise licence.
records.options: Run Postgres and Redis, set default_on guardrails, and test injection detection with a known attack set.

records.answer: The MCP gateway enforces allowed servers, tools and tool parameters per key, team, agent and organisation, per-server rate limits and per-server auth config (OAuth, OBO, API key, SigV4). MCP guardrails run pre_mcp_call on arguments and on tool descriptions during discovery, and post_mcp_call on results. Tool Policies classify tools seen in traffic as trusted, untrusted or blocked and block trust-chain violations.
records.gaps: General internet egress for agents is not controlled. Tool Policy overrides per team or key only block.
records.options: Route all agent tool traffic through the MCP gateway and control other egress at the network layer.

records.answer: Presidio guardrails mask or block PII entities per entity type on input, output and MCP calls, with confidence thresholds. Secret detection and redaction is an Enterprise guardrail. The docs reviewed do not describe enforcement of retrieval permissions per user or agent.

records.answer: Callers are identified as AI Consumers, resolved by an AI Auth Strategy from an API key or an OIDC token claim. Kong Identity issues client credentials whose client ID becomes the consumer's custom_id, giving a machine identity for an agent. Upstream agents are registered as AI Agent entities with an immutable name.
records.gaps: No documented link from a consumer identity to an owner, runtime or release version. Identity is per gateway caller, not a workload attestation.
records.options: Use labels and naming conventions to carry owner and release, or pair with a workload identity system such as SPIFFE and map its claims to consumers.

records.answer: Provider and upstream credentials are held in AI Vaults (HashiCorp Vault, AWS, GCP, Azure, CyberArk Conjur or the write-only Konnect Config Store) and resolved by reference at request time, so callers never see the provider key. The AI MCP OAuth2 plugin strips the caller's token before forwarding by default and can exchange it for a different token, cached until its expiry. Changelog 2.2.0 adds Token Vault support...
records.gaps: Rotation is left to the backing vault and cache settings. Token Vault has a changelog entry but no dedicated documentation page was found. Token exchange is Enterprise tier.
records.options: Use a dynamic secrets backend with short cache TTLs and test revocation propagation through the gateway cache grace period.

records.answer: The AI MCP OAuth2 plugin validates the user's token, then can exchange it as the subject token (with an optional actor token) for a token scoped to the upstream MCP server. It can also forward token claims, including nested claims, to the upstream as headers.
records.gaps: Documented for MCP traffic only. LLM and A2A delegation is not described. Requires Kong Gateway 3.14 or later and the AI Gateway Enterprise tier.
records.options: Test exchange against the target IdP (for example Okta, which needs the actor token) and confirm the downstream audit shows the original user.

records.answer: AI Agent entities of type a2a proxy A2A traffic and require callers to authenticate through an AI Auth Strategy (key-auth or OIDC). ACLs allow or deny AI Consumers, consumer groups or authenticated groups before traffic reaches the upstream agent, and the gateway can sign upstream requests with AWS SigV4.
records.gaps: Access is controlled at the agent level, not per skill. Upstream authentication beyond SigV4 is not described. The getting-started guide configures no authentication.
records.options: Configure OIDC auth strategies on every agent and test that a denied consumer gets 403 for agent card and message calls.

records.answer: Kong AI Gateway mediates network traffic and does not control actions an agent takes on its local host.
records.gaps: Checked the AI Gateway overview and entity pages. No local host controls.
records.options: Use the agent runtime or endpoint controls for local scopes.

records.answer: AI MCP Server ACLs filter tools/list and check each tools/call per consumer, consumer group or OAuth token claim, with deny rules winning. OAuth2 scoping can give write tools stricter access than read tools, and 2.1.0 added CEL allow_when and deny_when expressions. AI Models and AI Agents carry their own allow or deny ACLs.
records.gaps: Applies only to systems reached through the gateway. Tool annotations such as destructive do not change runtime behaviour.
records.options: Front every MCP server with a gateway listener and test that crafted calls to denied tools are rejected.

records.answer: AI Models route per consumer with ACLs and load balancing. AI Rate Limiting Advanced limits by tokens or cost per AI Consumer, consumer group, model or provider, including monthly calendar windows. Prompt screening comes from AI Prompt Guard, AI Semantic Prompt Guard and vendor guardrails (AWS, Azure, GCP Model Armor, Lakera, NeMo), and AI PII Sanitizer redacts prompts.
records.gaps: Cost limits apply to the next request, so one request can overrun. Model and provider matches need partition_by true or are not enforced. Semantic Prompt Guard is an allow and deny list, not a named injection detector.
records.options: Use Redis counters for shared limits and add a vendor guardrail for injection detection, then test with known jailbreak prompts.

records.answer: AI MCP Server entities convert REST APIs to MCP tools or proxy upstream MCP servers, validate tool calls against OpenAPI or JSON Schema parameters, enforce per-consumer tool ACLs and inbound OAuth2, and run attached rate limiting and logging policies. Outbound traffic can go through a forward proxy.
records.gaps: AI Guardrails are listed as not supported on MCP traffic, so tool calls and results are not injection screened. Annotations for destructive tools are hints only. No general internet egress allow list is described.

records.answer: AI PII Sanitizer masks PII in requests and responses through a separate PII service, with placeholder or synthetic replacement and custom regex patterns. records.gaps: Retrieval control covers only the gateway's own RAG Injector vector store. The RAG page gives conflicting examples on default ACL behaviour. PII service must be deployed separately.

records.answer: AI Agent entities enforce which consumers or groups may call each agent, detect A2A JSON-RPC and REST bindings, rewrite agent card URLs and limit request body size. Unknown schema properties in the entity config are rejected.
