records.answer: Agents are published as versioned solution packages (1.0.0, incremented on each republish) and deployed into Orchestrator folders. At run time a conversational agent executes as the signed-in user on UiPath-authenticated channels, or as an unattended robot account on anonymous channels. The documentation does not describe a distinct workload identity issued to each agent.
records.gaps: No per-agent identity linking owner, runtime and release. Audit records the user or robot account, not the agent. A shared robot account hides which agent acted.
records.options: Assign one robot account or external application per agent workload and record the mapping. Test what identity appears in Orchestrator audit for a Maestro-run agent.

records.answer: Integration Service connections hold OAuth access and refresh tokens and refresh them automatically, and can reference Orchestrator credential assets resolved at run time and cached for one hour. Orchestrator integrates external vaults (CyberArk, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp, AWS, Google, BeyondTrust, Delinea). MCP Remote server keys go in Secret assets referenced in headers. Serverless executions get a scoped bearer...
records.gaps: Rotation is documented only for the HashiCorp AD engine. The docs do not state that secrets are kept out of model context, and custom MCP code receives the bearer token and environment variables directly.
records.options: Use read-only vault stores with vault-side rotation. Test whether connection secrets or tokens can surface in agent traces or prompts.

records.answer: On UiPath-authenticated channels a conversational agent runs under the user's own identity. Personal connections let an agent call downstream systems such as Outlook, Slack or Salesforce with the user's own connection, with fallback to the shared folder connection. Tool processes must be set to inherit the parent job identity.
records.gaps: Personal connections are Public Preview and unsupported for external application token channels. Autonomous and anonymous runs use a robot account, so the initiating user is not propagated. Fallback to a shared connection silently drops the user context.
records.options: Disable shared fallback connections for user-context tools. Test what identity the downstream system logs for a personal versus shared connection.

records.answer: Agent Gateway (preview) registers external A2A agents and MCP servers as platform resources, and UiPath conversational agents expose an A2A agent card inbound. Maestro calls a remote A2A agent through the Invoke an Agent activity, which needs an Agent 2 Agent Integration Service connection and selects skills from the remote Agent Card.
records.gaps: The fetched pages do not describe the A2A authentication methods, authorisation of inbound callers or trust boundary rules. Agent Gateway is in preview.
records.options: Read the Agent 2 Agent authentication page before relying on it. Test inbound A2A calls with an unauthorised token.

records.answer: Delegate is a desktop agent that acts with the user's access on their machine. Admins can set and lock approval mode, execution mode, screen context, blocked apps and sites, and tool permissions through Automation Ops. Guarded mode limits the agent to a project's allowed files and folders. Robot policies in Automation Ops apply Runtime Analyzer rules that restrict applications and web pages.
records.gaps: Guarded mode is experimental and Delegate documentation is preview status. Low-code agents run on Serverless robots with no documented local scope controls.
records.options: Lock Delegate execution mode centrally and test that blocked apps cannot be driven through Computer Use.

records.answer: Agents reach connected systems only through tools configured in Agent Builder, using Integration Service connections scoped to Orchestrator folders with Create and Edit permissions. Folder roles and robot account assignments set what the executing identity can do. Tool guardrails can block or filter tool calls on input and output conditions.
records.gaps: No agent-specific scope beneath the executing identity. UiPath states nothing can give a coding agent less than its identity allows. Connector OAuth scopes are fixed for UiPath public apps unless you bring your own app.
records.options: Use bring-your-own OAuth apps with minimal scopes and dedicated folders per agent. Test a blocked tool guardrail condition.

records.answer: Escalations send a task to a named recipient through Action Center apps, and each outcome maps to Continue or End. Tool guardrails can escalate a specific tool call before execution based on its inputs, which binds the decision to the proposed call. A Studio Web policy can require at least one human-in-the-loop escalation before publishing. Delegate asks for confirmation on data-changing actions.
records.gaps: Prompt-triggered escalations are non-deterministic. Replay handling and timeouts are not documented. Escalation memory (preview) can reuse a past human resolution without raising a new escalation.
records.options: Use tool guardrail escalation rather than prompt-based escalation for consequential actions. Disable escalation memory where each approval must be fresh.

records.answer: Agents are published to a feed, deployed as solutions into folders, and moved between versions with Change version. Studio Web design policies block publishing of agents that fail minimum score, temperature, token, iteration or HITL limits. The AI Trust Layer Enable Agents toggle turns agents on or off per tenant. Instance management covers terminating agents and agent jobs.
records.gaps: No documented approval step on publish. Identity creation for agents relies on manual robot account and folder setup.
records.options: Route publishing through CI/CD with a review gate. Audit robot account folder assignments.

records.answer: Maestro orchestrates agents, robots and people in BPMN processes. Instance management offers pause, resume, retry from the last completed step, cancel, go to and migrate to another process version. An action history records who performed each action, plus system events such as throttling.
records.gaps: Cancel is irreversible and deletes attached human tasks. Maestro does not record an actor-type field.
records.options: Test retry and migrate on a faulted instance in a non-production folder.

records.answer: All LLM traffic goes through the AI Trust Layer gateway. Policies restrict which UiPath-managed providers and models each product can call, can lock current model versions by turning off auto allow, can require bring-your-own model only, and restrict routing regions including Australia. UiPath states data is not used to train third-party models. Studio Web policy caps temperature and tokens per response.
records.gaps: Custom LLM configurations bypass the Models tab restrictions. Policy changes take up to five minutes to apply.
records.options: Set LLM region routing to Australia and disable auto allow new models. Confirm the region in the audit log Model Location field.

records.answer: Agent jobs run on Serverless robots through Unified Runtime on UiPath-managed infrastructure. For Coded and Command MCP servers UiPath describes isolated ephemeral containers without elevated privileges, with timeouts and resource limits. Delegate runs on the user's own Windows machine.
records.gaps: No documented egress filtering or network isolation detail. UiPath does not sandbox custom code logic and leaves network controls to the customer.
records.options: Ask UiPath for container network egress documentation. Test outbound calls from a Command MCP server.

records.answer: Conversational agent chat history is scoped to the tenant and users see only history for agents they can use. Maestro variables are scoped to one process instance. Agent traces hold run state with a tenant TTL setting of off (90 days), 1 or 7 days.
records.gaps: No documented session resumption controls or per-session retention for chat history.
records.options: Set the trace TTL policy and confirm how long chat history persists.

records.answer: Unified Runtime is the shared engine that runs low-code and coded agents and their tool calls on Serverless robots. Studio Web policy caps iterations per execution between 1 and 100. Tool guardrails run in order before or after each tool call.
records.gaps: Harness internals are not documented.
records.options: Set maximum iterations by policy and review traces for tool call order.

records.answer: Agent memory (preview) offers episodic memory of past cases and feedback, and escalation memory of human resolutions. Memory spaces can be shared across agents, and items can be inspected and deleted in Agents instance management. Customer managed key encryption is set when a space is created.
records.gaps: Preview feature. The memory page does not describe access control or a retention policy. Memory items cannot be edited, only deleted and re-added.
records.options: Restrict who can manage memory spaces and review stored items before production.

records.answer: The AI Trust Layer LLM gateway applies policies at tenant, group or user level before requests reach models. It enforces product and model allow lists, region routing, a prompt injection guardrail, harmful content and IP protection checks, and third-party guardrail vendors. Conversational agents have a per-user monthly usage limit.
records.gaps: No per-agent policy level, quota or rate limit is documented. Context Grounding honours only tenant-level policies.
records.options: Use groups to approximate per-workload policies. Test the prompt injection guardrail with known payloads.

records.answer: Tool guardrails apply log, filter, block or escalate actions to tool inputs and outputs using string, number and boolean rules. Centralized guardrails can apply at tool level. MCP server management is governed by Orchestrator roles, and the MCP OAuth flow fails closed unless dynamic client registration is enabled, with a callback domain allow list. Workflow Analyzer rules restrict allowed packages and activities.
records.gaps: No documented internet egress control, per-tool quota or rate limit. Tool guardrails are configured per agent, not as a central tool allow list.
records.options: Restrict MCP server creation to a dedicated role. Test block and filter guardrails against a sample tool.

records.answer: In-flight PII masking replaces detected entities with placeholders in agent prompts and runtime files before the LLM call and restores them in the response. Tool guardrail filter actions remove fields from tool inputs or outputs. Restrict Insights Trace data limits what reaches Insights.
records.gaps: Entity list lacks Australian identifiers such as TFN or Medicare number. Masking is off by default and needs an eligible tier. No per-agent retrieval authorisation for Context Grounding is documented.
records.options: Use a bring-your-own guardrail vendor for Australian entities. Test masking with synthetic records.

records.answer: Agent Gateway (preview) is the central place where external A2A agents are registered before Maestro flows and agents can use them. Outbound calls need an Agent 2 Agent connection to each remote agent.
records.gaps: No documented policy on allowed agent pairs, message schemas or inbound callers. Enforcement beyond connection permissions is not described.
records.options: Limit who can create Agent 2 Agent connections. Ask UiPath whether Agent Gateway will enforce pair policies.

records.answer: Action Center escalations let a named person review and resolve agent work, with outcomes that continue or end the run. Studio Web policy can require a human-in-the-loop step before an agent is published. The Agents hub has a Feedback tab for trace review and feedback capture.
records.gaps: Prompt-based escalations depend on the agent deciding to escalate.
records.options: Use deterministic Maestro user tasks for mandatory review points.

records.answer: The Agents hub alerts on errors, health score degradation and poor runtime evaluation scores. Agent review (preview) grades an agent A to F against best practices. Episodic memory feeds past cases and feedback into later runs.
records.gaps: Anomaly detection is limited to time-based views for manual review. Health score calculation is not documented.
records.options: Build evaluation sets from runtime traces and track scores per release.

records.answer: Agent unit consumption reports rank agents by usage, and traces show a usage badge on each billable model run span. The AI Trust Layer usage summary counts LLM actions per product and status.
records.gaps: No monetary cost, token cost, labour saving or ROI reporting in the fetched pages.
records.options: Combine agent unit data with business outcome data outside UiPath.

records.answer: The Agents Overview tab shows total jobs, success rate, average response time and unit consumption, with alerts on errors. Maestro shows running and faulted instance counts, an incidents table and throttling events.
records.gaps: No infrastructure load metrics for Serverless robots or automated anomaly detection documented.
records.options: Export run data and alert on latency and failure thresholds externally.

records.answer: Checked the Agents hub, Agent Gateway and MCP pages. Agent Gateway lists registered MCP servers and A2A agents, but no view shows an agent's reach and action scopes against downstream systems. UiPath's MCP guidance tells customers to keep their own inventory of agent tools.
records.gaps: No connectivity map of agents, tools, connections and permissions.
records.options: Build a map from Orchestrator folder, connection and MCP server APIs.

records.answer: The AI Trust Layer audit log records date, product, feature, tenant, user, model, model location, status and, when enabled, full prompts and outputs. Orchestrator audit records actions by user and component. Agent traces hold tool inputs, outputs and decisions. Maestro records an action history with who acted.
records.gaps: Documentation does not state that logs are tamper-proof (only the product page claims tamper-evident). No agent field in the AI Trust Layer audit. Prompt saving can be turned off, and trace TTL can be 1 day.
records.options: Export audit data to a write-once store. Keep input and output saving on for audited agents.

records.answer: UiPath describes a unified schema-based audit system that can feed Splunk or Microsoft Sentinel. AI Trust Layer audit can be exported on Enterprise plans, and Orchestrator audit exports to CSV and monthly archives.
records.gaps: No documented native detections or response ownership. AI Trust Layer exports with prompts are limited to four per month. The streaming mechanism for unified audit was not found in the fetched docs.
records.options: Pull audit logs through the API on a schedule into the SIEM and write detections there.

records.answer: AI Trust Layer policies control which providers and model versions products may call and can lock current versions. UiPath holds ISO/IEC 42001 certification for its AI management system, per its product page.
records.gaps: No model file inspection, lineage record or AI bill of materials for customers. Certification evidence is a vendor claim on a product page.
records.options: Request the ISO 42001 certificate and model provider list through the UiPath Trust Center.

records.answer: UiPath states its serverless containers are isolated, ephemeral and run without elevated privileges, with timeouts and resource limits. The product page lists SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and IRAP among certifications.
records.gaps: No customer-visible runtime attestation or host hardening detail. Certifications are listed on a product page, not verified.
records.options: Obtain the SOC 2 Type II report and IRAP assessment through the Trust Center.

records.answer: Studio Web policy can restrict packages and activities by allow or block list and control activity feeds and preview packages. UiPath's MCP guidance makes code review, dependency scanning and endpoint vetting a customer duty.
records.gaps: No SBOM, scanning or review of MCP servers or coded tools by UiPath. Guidance is advice, not a control.
records.options: Scan Coded MCP server packages in CI before publishing with the uipath-mcp CLI.

records.answer: Checked the MCP compliance guidelines, Agent Gateway and Marketplace references. No scanning for squatting, tool metadata poisoning or package compromise is documented. UiPath's 2025.10 post describes supply chain risk detection work with Noma Security as ongoing.
records.gaps: No native third-party tool scanning.
records.options: Use a third-party MCP scanner before registering Remote servers.

records.answer: Context Grounding indexes are created in Orchestrator, and the Agents hub shows index status, health and ingestion progress. The AI Trust Layer policy can disable Context Grounding at tenant level.
records.gaps: The fetched governance page does not describe index access control, sanitisation or retention.
records.options: Read the Orchestrator indexes documentation and test folder permissions on indexes.

records.answer: Checked the security and governance product page, the 2025.10 governance post and Agents docs. UiPath blocks unapproved model calls inside its own platform, but no discovery of AI use outside UiPath is documented. AI asset discovery is mentioned only as ongoing work with Noma Security.
records.gaps: No shadow AI discovery.
records.options: Use a dedicated AI discovery tool alongside UiPath.

records.answer: Checked guardrails, evaluations and the product page. UiPath cites AIUC-1 adversarial testing by Schellman of its own agents, but offers no customer tool for automated adversarial testing. Evaluation sets measure quality, not attacks.
records.gaps: No automated AI pen-testing capability.
records.options: Run an external red-teaming tool against published agents in a test tenant.

records.answer: The Agents page is described as a centralized registry of deployed and draft UiPath agents. Agent Gateway registers MCP servers and A2A agents, including external ones. Solution packages are held in the tenant feed.
records.gaps: No owner, schema or software component records documented. External agents appear only if registered.
records.options: Export agent and server lists through the API into a CMDB.

records.answer: Automation Hub has an Agentic AI idea flow: an employee submits an assessment, an Idea Approver approves or rejects, the Process Owner completes a detailed assessment, and a Program Manager decides in the Decision Pipeline. Publishing is gated by Studio Web design policies.
records.gaps: Automation Hub approval is not technically linked to publishing. No registration approval for tools or models.
records.options: Require an approved Automation Hub idea ID in the CI/CD publish step.

records.answer: The Agents hub reports guardrail activity across deployed agents and alerts on degraded health. The AI Trust Layer usage summary shows LLM actions by status, including policy blocks. A uipath-governance coding agent skill (Public Preview) checks policy compliance against standards such as ISO 42001.
records.gaps: No consolidated control coverage or risk dashboard. The compliance skill is preview.
records.options: Trial the governance skill against a test tenant and compare with manual review.

records.answer: Automation Ops holds governance policies for the AI Trust Layer, Studio Web, Studio, Robot and Assistant, deployed at tenant, group or user level. A coding agent skill can author and deploy policies.
records.gaps: Policy versioning, ownership, review and change history are not described in the governance page.
records.options: Manage policy definitions in source control with the governance skill and record reviews there.

records.answer: Automation Hub moves agent ideas from submission through assessment and decision. Agents are then evaluated, published as versioned packages, deployed, upgraded or downgraded, and terminated through instance management.
records.gaps: The stages sit in separate products with no documented link. Retirement steps are not described.
records.options: Track lifecycle state against the Automation Hub idea record.

records.answer: Automation Hub assigns a Process Owner to each agentic idea, who completes the detailed assessment.
records.gaps: The Agents hub does not show an owner for deployed agents, models or tools.
records.options: Record agent owners in solution metadata or an external register.

records.answer: The Automation Hub Agentic AI assessment captures agent type, scope, escalation points and success measures, and computes an idea score.
records.gaps: The assessment has no dedicated risk or data sensitivity questions and does not map risk levels to controls.
records.options: Add custom risk questions to the assessment if the tenant allows it.

records.answer: Agent versions increment on each publish, and Change version upgrades or rolls back a solution deployment. Design policies apply to each new version before republishing. Model versions can be locked by turning off auto allow new models.
records.gaps: No native approval of changes. Rollback does not recover deleted resource data. Prompt, permission and knowledge changes are not versioned separately.
records.options: Use the CLI in CI/CD with a review gate and test rollback in a test deployment.

records.answer: Checked Automation Ops governance, AI Trust Layer policy and Automation Hub pages. No register for policy exceptions or accepted risks is documented.
records.gaps: No exception recording, approval or expiry.
records.options: Record exceptions in a GRC tool.

records.answer: AI Trust Layer policy sets trace TTL (off, 1 or 7 days), can stop saving prompts and outputs to audit, and restricts LLM region routing. Audit logs have tiered retention up to 3 years. UiPath states data is not used for third-party training.
records.gaps: Memory and chat history retention are not documented. TTL choices are fixed.
records.options: Confirm Australian data residency for tenant data and LLM routing with UiPath.

records.answer: Audit logs and traces can be exported or reviewed for audit reports. The governance skill checks policy compliance against ISO 42001 or ISO 27001 (Public Preview). UiPath lists certifications including ISO 42001, SOC 2 Type II and IRAP.
records.gaps: No evidence library mapping controls to requirements.
records.options: Map exported audit evidence to controls in a GRC tool.

records.answer: AI Trust Layer policy can switch model providers on or off, require bring-your-own models only, and add third-party guardrail vendors. MCP OAuth needs an allow list of callback domains.
records.gaps: No periodic reassessment or retirement workflow for external models, tools or services. MCP vetting is left to customers.
records.options: Review enabled providers and Remote MCP servers on a schedule.

records.answer: Langfuse records agent activity as traces with observation types such as agent and tool, but it does not issue or manage agent or workload identities. Names on observations are application-supplied labels.
records.gaps: No identity linking an agent to an owner, runtime or release. Observation names and trace version fields are free text set by the instrumented application.
records.options: Use an identity platform for agent identity and pass the identifier into trace metadata or tags so Langfuse traces can be correlated.

records.answer: Langfuse stores LLM provider credentials, encrypted with ENCRYPTION_KEY, only for its own playground and evaluator calls. It does not broker credentials to agents or their tools.
records.gaps: LLM connections serve Langfuse features only. Key rotation for ENCRYPTION_KEY is not documented.
records.options: Use a secrets manager or credential broker for agents. Treat Langfuse project API keys as secrets in that broker.

records.answer: Langfuse can attach a userId attribute to traces for analytics, but it does not propagate user identity or delegated authority to downstream services.
records.gaps: userId is an unauthenticated label supplied by the application.
records.options: Implement OBO in the identity provider or gateway and record the resulting user identifier on traces.

records.answer: Langfuse traces multi-agent workflows and draws agent graphs, but it does not authenticate or authorise communication between agents.
records.gaps: No A2A authentication or trust boundary controls.
records.options: Use an A2A-capable gateway or agent platform. Langfuse can trace the resulting calls.

records.answer: Langfuse is an observability and evaluation platform and does not control what agents may do on a local host. Checked the observability, guardrails and self-hosting documentation.
records.gaps: No local action scoping.
records.options: Use the agent harness or host sandbox for local scopes and trace tool calls into Langfuse.

records.answer: Langfuse does not grant or restrict agent actions against connected systems. Its RBAC scopes govern Langfuse users and API keys, not agents.
records.gaps: No remote action scoping for agents.
records.options: Enforce remote scopes in a tool gateway or the target systems.

records.answer: Annotation queues let humans score outputs after the fact, but there is no pre-execution approval bound to a proposed agent action, with denial or replay handling.
records.gaps: Human review is retrospective scoring, not an approval gate.
records.options: Implement approval in the agent framework or orchestration layer and log approvals as Langfuse scores or events.

records.answer: SCIM and the Organization API provision human users, memberships, projects and project API keys (Enterprise). They do not manage agent identities or agent permissions.
records.gaps: No agent provisioning or retirement.
records.options: Use an agent platform or identity provider for agent lifecycle. Langfuse project API keys could be issued per agent through the Organization API.

records.answer: Langfuse observes workflows built in frameworks such as LangGraph but does not sequence, cancel or retry agent workflows.
records.gaps: No orchestration runtime.
records.options: Use an orchestration framework and instrument it with Langfuse.

records.answer: Langfuse does not serve inference for applications. LLM connections call external providers only for the playground, prompt experiments and LLM-as-a-Judge.
records.gaps: Model version and endpoint are recorded on generations when the application sends them, but Langfuse does not enforce them.
records.options: Use a model provider or gateway for inference and record model and parameters on generation observations.

records.answer: Langfuse does not provide an execution environment, code interpreter or network control for agents.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use a sandbox or container platform for agent execution.

records.answer: Langfuse sessions group traces from one conversation for replay and scoring. They are an observability record, not agent session state the agent reads or resumes from.
records.gaps: No agent-facing session state store.
records.options: Use the agent framework's state store and propagate sessionId into Langfuse for correlation.

records.answer: Langfuse does not execute tools. It records tool observations emitted by the application's harness.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use an agent framework or harness and instrument tool calls with the tool observation type.

records.answer: Langfuse retains trace history for analysis, but it is not long-term memory that agents use across sessions.
records.gaps: No agent memory service.
records.options: Use a dedicated memory store and trace its reads and writes as retriever observations.

records.answer: Langfuse does not route or rate-limit model traffic. Its documentation points to gateways such as LiteLLM, OpenRouter or Portkey, and its cost data can feed external rate limiting through the Metrics API.
records.gaps: No routing, quota or injection screening enforcement.
records.options: Deploy a model gateway and send its traces and costs to Langfuse.

records.answer: Langfuse does not enforce allowed tools, schemas or egress. The guardrails page states run-time protection comes from third-party libraries and Langfuse evaluates them after the fact.
records.gaps: No tool gateway.
records.options: Use a tool or MCP gateway and trace its decisions as guardrail observations.

records.answer: Langfuse does not mediate retrieval or apply DLP to agent data flows. Its masking hooks redact telemetry inside the SDK before export to Langfuse, which protects the trace store but not the agent's data access.
records.gaps: Masking applies only to data sent to Langfuse, and no server-side masking is described.
records.options: Use a data gateway or DLP service for retrieval, and configure SDK masking to keep sensitive data out of traces.

records.answer: Langfuse has no control over which agents may talk to each other.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use an A2A gateway or agent platform policy.

records.answer: Annotation queues let reviewers score and comment on traces, observations or sessions against defined score configs, with assignment of users and optional corrected outputs. Queues can be managed by API. Session pages also allow UI scoring.
records.gaps: The annotation queue page does not state tier availability. Review is after execution.
records.options: Confirm tier on the pricing page and pilot a queue with domain reviewers comparing against LLM-as-a-Judge scores.

records.answer: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators run continuously on matching production observations with filters and sampling. Datasets and experiments support offline validation against versioned test sets. Alerts fire on threshold breaches of scores, cost or latency over a time window.
records.gaps: Anomaly detection is threshold-based only. No statistical baselining is documented. Trace-level evaluators are deprecated on Cloud from 16 November 2026.
records.options: Build evaluators per risk, calibrate against human labels, and route alerts to Slack or signed webhooks.

records.answer: Langfuse calculates token usage and USD cost per generation from ingested values or model price definitions, with pricing tiers, dashboards by model, tag or user, and cost alerts. It does not cover infrastructure or labour cost, savings or output yield.
records.gaps: Only model token cost. Reasoning models need ingested counts. Price changes apply only to later generations.
records.options: Export cost via the Metrics API or blob export and join with infrastructure and business data in a BI tool.

records.answer: Dashboards show application latency including P95 and P99, request counts and throughput, and alerts can fire on latency thresholds. Langfuse does not monitor host or container load.
records.gaps: Application-level latency only. No infrastructure metrics or anomaly models.
records.options: Pair with an APM or infrastructure monitoring tool. Langfuse accepts OpenTelemetry spans for correlation.

records.answer: Agent graphs render a trace's agent, tool and retriever steps as a graph, aggregated or expanded. This shows what an agent did in observed runs, not its full reach or potential action scopes against downstream systems.
records.gaps: Only executed paths appear. No inventory of connected systems or permissions.
records.options: Combine with a tool inventory or gateway configuration to show potential reach.

records.answer: Traces record inputs, outputs, tool calls and user and session identifiers. Enterprise audit logs record administrative actions by user or API key with before and after state, and are described as immutable. Trace data can be deleted by users with permission and through retention.
records.gaps: Immutability of audit logs is asserted but the mechanism is not documented. Trace records are deletable, so they are not a tamper-proof ledger. Audit log retention period is not stated.
records.options: Export traces and audit logs to write-once blob storage with object lock, and restrict traces:delete scope.

records.answer: Traces carry user and session correlation and can be exported to S3 or Azure Blob every 20 minutes or longer for SIEM ingestion. SDK masking redacts fields before export. Langfuse provides no security detections or response workflow itself, and traces third-party guardrails rather than detecting attacks.
records.gaps: No native SIEM connector or security detection content. Detection depends on evaluators and external guardrails.
records.options: Ship blob exports to the SIEM, build detections on guardrail and evaluator scores, and assign alert ownership in the SOC.

records.answer: Langfuse does not inspect model files, track model lineage or produce an AI BoM. Model definitions hold pricing match patterns only.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use a model scanning or AI BoM tool.

records.answer: Langfuse does not assure inference or tool execution containers or hosts.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use container and host security tooling.

records.answer: Langfuse does not scan or review MCP servers, CLIs or extensions. It publishes its own MCP server with project-scoped keys, which is a component to assess rather than an assurance feature.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Assess the Langfuse MCP server and SDKs in the organisation's own tool assurance process.

records.answer: Langfuse does not scan third-party registries, plugins or packages for squatting or poisoning.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use a supply chain or MCP scanning tool.

records.answer: Langfuse datasets are versioned evaluation test sets, not governed data or feature stores for agents. Retention does not apply to datasets.
records.gaps: No sanitisation or governance of production data stores.
records.options: Govern data and feature stores in a data platform. Treat Langfuse datasets as data needing their own handling.

records.answer: Langfuse only sees applications that are instrumented to send it traces, so it cannot discover shadow AI.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use network, SaaS or endpoint discovery tools.

records.answer: Langfuse does not generate adversarial attacks. Experiments can run an application against a dataset, which could hold adversarial prompts supplied by the user.
records.gaps: No attack generation or boundary testing.
records.options: Use a red-teaming tool and log its runs to Langfuse datasets and experiments for comparison.

records.answer: Langfuse keeps a central prompt registry with versions and labels, and a list of model definitions for pricing. It does not register agents or tools, schemas or software components.
records.gaps: Inventory covers prompts and model price entries only.
records.options: Use an asset registry for agents and tools and link entries to Langfuse prompt names.

records.answer: There is no submission and approval workflow for models, agents or tools. Protected labels restrict who can promote a prompt version but are not an approval workflow.
records.gaps: No approval records.
records.options: Run approvals in a GRC or ticketing tool and restrict protected label changes to approvers.

records.answer: Dashboards report quality, cost and latency metrics, not control coverage, policy breaches or governance status.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Feed evaluator scores into a governance reporting tool.

records.answer: Langfuse has no feature for authoring, versioning or publishing AI policies.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use a GRC or policy management tool.

records.answer: Prompts move through labelled versions for environments such as staging and production, and experiments on versioned datasets test changes before promotion. Langfuse does not track models, agents or use cases from proposal to retirement.
records.gaps: Lifecycle covers prompt testing and deployment only.
records.options: Use an AI lifecycle or GRC tool for use cases and link prompt versions and experiment runs as evidence.

records.answer: Langfuse assigns roles to people for organisations and projects but has no owner field for agents, models or tools.
records.gaps: No accountable owner records.
records.options: Record ownership in an asset registry and use project boundaries to align teams.

records.answer: Langfuse has no use case risk assessment or classification feature.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use a GRC or AI governance tool.

records.answer: Prompts are versioned automatically, served by label, and rolled back by moving the production label. Protected labels stop members and viewers changing production (Enterprise, Pro with Teams add-on, self-hosted EE). Audit logs capture prompt changes on Enterprise. Changes to models, tools, permissions and knowledge are not governed.
records.gaps: No approval step before a label change. Coverage is prompts only.
records.options: Gate label changes through CI using the API and restrict protected labels to release managers.

records.answer: Langfuse has no feature for recording or approving policy exceptions or accepted risks.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use a GRC tool.

records.answer: Project retention deletes traces, observations, scores and media nightly after a set period (Pro, Enterprise, self-hosted EE). Deletion APIs remove traces, projects and accounts. Cloud offers separate US, EU, Japan and HIPAA regions, and self-hosting allows any location. This governs Langfuse's own copy of data, not agent inputs, outputs or memory elsewhere.
records.gaps: Retention does not cover datasets or audit logs. No permitted-use controls. ClickHouse trace data is not replicated cross-region.
records.options: Set retention per project, mask sensitive fields in the SDK, choose region or self-host, and delete datasets separately.

records.answer: Langfuse holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 for its own service, but the product does not map evidence to control requirements. Traces, scores and audit logs can be exported as raw evidence.
records.gaps: No evidence collection or traceability to requirements.
records.options: Use a GRC tool to collect Langfuse exports and vendor reports as evidence.

records.answer: Langfuse has no feature for approving or reassessing external models, tools or services. LLM connections configure providers without an approval process.
records.gaps: Outside product category.
records.options: Use a third-party risk management tool, and restrict llmApiKeys scopes to admins.

records.answer: Agent Builder custom agents have a unique agent ID set at creation, and the creating user is recorded as owner. Workloads calling Elasticsearch authenticate with API keys that carry metadata and show the creating user and realm. Neither links an agent to a runtime or release version.
records.gaps: No release or runtime binding. No agent versioning documented. Agents are not first-class Elasticsearch principals.
records.options: Map each agent to a dedicated API key with metadata naming owner and release, and track releases in an external registry.

records.answer: LLM provider and MCP server credentials sit in inference endpoints or connectors, not in prompts. The MCP connector supports Secret-type headers that are encrypted. Elasticsearch API keys support optional expiry and deletion by owners or administrators. Rotation is not described on the API key page.
records.gaps: API keys have no expiry by default. MCP connector auth is static headers only, no OAuth. No documented automatic rotation or short-lived per-call credentials.
records.options: Set expiry on all keys, rotate through automation, and test that secrets never appear in conversation or trace data.

records.answer: Agent Builder tools run Elasticsearch requests with the privileges of the current user or API key, so DLS and FLS apply per user. On Serverless, MCP clients connecting with OAuth 2.1 act with the authorising user's live permissions. Elasticsearch also supports run_as impersonation through the es-security-runas-user header. User identity is not propagated to external MCP servers, which receive static connector...
records.gaps: OAuth for the MCP server is Serverless only. API key callers share one identity. No user propagation to external MCP or third-party services.
records.options: Use OAuth on Serverless or per-user API keys, and front external MCP servers with an OBO-capable gateway.

records.answer: Agent Builder exposes agents over the A2A protocol with a metadata endpoint and a protocol endpoint, both requiring an API key. A read-only key can limit what the calling agent can do. The page documents no per-agent trust boundary or mutual authentication.
records.gaps: API key only. No allowlist of caller agents and no agent card signing documented. Streaming unsupported and confirmation prompts cannot be answered over A2A.
records.options: Issue one scoped API key per calling agent and place an A2A gateway in front for pairing policy.

records.answer: Elastic's agent and retrieval products do not run agents on a local host or expose local filesystem or shell actions. Checked the Agent Builder overview, custom tools and limitations pages, which list Elasticsearch, workflow and MCP tools only.
records.gaps: No local host action scoping.
records.options: Use the agent host or coding tool's own sandbox controls.

records.answer: A request through Agent Builder must pass Kibana feature privileges, Elasticsearch cluster and index privileges and Kibana space scope. Tools run with the caller's privileges, and API keys cannot exceed their owner's rights. Each agent is assigned only selected tools, and index search tools are limited to named indices or patterns. DLS and FLS further restrict documents and fields.
records.gaps: Scopes on external MCP servers depend on the connector's static credentials. DLS has documented query limits and aggregation leakage.
records.options: Keep per-agent API keys with narrow index patterns, and test DLS against aggregation queries.

records.answer: Custom tools can require user confirmation with never, once or always settings. In the UI this applies to workflow and MCP tools, and through the Tools API to all custom tool types. Confirmation applies only to agent calls, direct Tools API calls skip it, and sub-agents decline confirmation-requiring actions.
records.gaps: Generally available on Serverless only, planned for Stack. Bulk-imported MCP tools default to never. Binding to exact arguments and replay handling are not documented.
records.options: Set confirmation to always for write tools and test argument tampering after approval.

records.answer: Custom agents are created, edited and deleted in Agent Builder with Public, Shared or Private access and per-agent User, Editor or Manager grants. Deletion is restricted to the owner, administrators or Managers in 9.5 and later. API keys are created, updated and deleted through the security APIs.
records.gaps: No approval step or change history for agent creation documented. Defaults differ by version, Public on Stack 9.4 to 9.5.
records.options: Manage agents and keys through the Kibana APIs from a reviewed pipeline, and set Private as standard.

packages.name: AI use discovery and safe-use boundaries
packages.prerequisite: Sponsor authorises bounded discovery and assigns owners to unknowns.
packages.completion_evidence: A reconciled sample inventory, permitted-use guidance and risk triage record, with unknown coverage visible.
packages.do_not_progress_if: No person accepts responsibility for the use or its data boundary.

packages.name: Controlled assistance and task adoption
packages.prerequisite: Approved tools and tasks, support contact and authorised sources exist.
packages.completion_evidence: Users demonstrate safe task completion and escalation, with baseline effort and rework recorded.
packages.do_not_progress_if: Users cannot identify unacceptable outputs or sensitive input restrictions.

packages.name: Measured pilot and go or stop evidence
packages.prerequisite: Representative authorised data, task owner, test environment and agreed acceptance criteria.
packages.completion_evidence: Baseline comparison includes failure cases, harms, review effort and documented release recommendation.
packages.do_not_progress_if: Material risk, permission or evidence gaps remain without accountable acceptance.

packages.name: Production readiness and service support
packages.prerequisite: A pilot has accepted task evidence and operational ownership.
packages.completion_evidence: End-to-end exception, denial, fallback, support and change exercises meet the client's task requirements.
packages.do_not_progress_if: The service cannot be stopped, supported or recovered by authorised staff.

packages.name: Shared controls and accountable enterprise scale
packages.prerequisite: Several uses have functioning local owners, service evidence and shared-platform visibility.
packages.completion_evidence: Shared dependencies, costs and exceptions reconcile to local use cases with exercised escalation and failure boundaries.
packages.do_not_progress_if: Central approval replaces local accountability or supplier concentration lacks a credible contingency.

packages.name: Operating assurance, optimisation and replacement
packages.prerequisite: Operating outcomes, failures, changes and costs are measurable with sufficient history.
packages.completion_evidence: Independent challenge and regression evidence support an improvement, replacement or retirement decision.
packages.do_not_progress_if: An optimisation improves one measure while breaching accepted harm, permission or service limits.

concerns.concern: How does agent-to-agent (A2A) authorisation work, and how do we stop one agent acting with another agent's permissions?
concerns.summary: Your Okta agent identities from c4-1 are the strongest base, because Okta lets one agent call another under the target's identity with scoped tokens and enforces this at token issuance. Claude Code has no cryptographic agent authentication for agent-to-agent traffic, and Wiz and Purview do not address the channel, so nothing in your stack inspects messages on the wire. To stop one agent borrowing another's permissions, give every agent its own identity, restrict allowed callers per target, and add a gateway if you need message-path enforcement.
next_steps: Register each agent separately in Okta with its own workload principal and create agent-to-agent connections only for approved caller and callee pairs.
Test a two-agent chain in Okta and confirm the System Log shows both identities, then test a caller with no connection is refused.
Test multi-hop delegation explicitly, since Okta does not describe chains beyond one hop.
Keep Claude Code agent teams disabled in managed settings unless needed, and decide whether cross-boundary agent traffic needs an external A2A gateway.
unknowns: Whether Okta enforces anything on the message path, as only token issuance enforcement is documented.
Whether Okta supports the A2A protocol itself or cross-organisation trust boundaries, which its records do not describe.
How your AWS AgentCore deployment is configured, as no tenant or Region was tested.
Whether Wiz and Purview add anything to A2A authorisation. Their records show no A2A authentication or authorisation, and Purview only audits interactions after the fact.
Whether the Claude Code agent teams feature is currently enabled in your environment.

claims.text: Okta's Connect to another AI agent resource connection lets one agent call another under the target's identity through an authorisation server and audience with allowed scopes. This is the in-stack mechanism that keeps a caller from simply reusing the callee's permissions.

Okta's agent-to-agent connections define which agents may call which, but enforcement happens at token issuance. There is no inline gateway for A2A traffic and no message schema enforcement described, so support is partial.

Okta Agent Gateway exchanges the agent token for downstream tokens on behalf of the user, and a linked app restricts an agent to acting for users currently signed in. Downstream apps must implement the ID-JAG grant, and delegation chains beyond one hop are not described.

Claude Code agent teams pass messages through local mailbox files between sessions of the same user on one machine. There is no cryptographic authentication of agents or trust boundary definition, and the feature is experimental and off by default, so support is partial.

Claude Code's RFC 8693 act chain exists only in self-hosted environments, and Anthropic advises treating the session token as weaker than a direct login. Local sessions pass the developer's own credentials rather than a delegated, attenuated token.

AWS AgentCore Runtime supports A2A communication, but the assessment notes that discovery and protocol interoperability do not confer authority. Peer endpoints should be pinned and caller identity verified.

AWS Gateway documents passthrough targets including A2A, but protocol support alone does not prove pairwise delegation restrictions. Peers need authenticating and unapproved agent pairs denying, and no deployed configuration was tested.

Alternative: Kong AI Gateway AI Agent entities enforce which consumers or groups may call each agent and detect A2A JSON-RPC bindings. It has no skill-level ACLs, does not validate payloads beyond envelope detection, and allowed pairs depend on each calling agent having its own consumer identity.

Alternative: Microsoft Entra Agent ID uses Conditional Access scoped by agent identity or blueprint to decide which agents get tokens for a callee, and risk policies can block risky agents. Enforcement is at token issuance, not on the message path.

Alternative: Ping Identity Agent Privilege places remote agents behind an AI gateway with policy on which operations agents can use, and AI Guard inspects agent-to-agent traffic. A broader allowed-pairs matrix is not described.

concerns.concern: What gateway do we need in front of models and MCP tools?
concerns.summary: The client's stack already has partial gateway coverage, but no single product covers both models and MCP tools. Claude Code's own gateway and AWS Gateway are the main model and tool candidates, while Okta covers MCP traffic only and Wiz and Purview do not act as gateways. Gaps remain in prompt injection screening, rate limits and schema validation, so the client needs a model gateway with fail-closed settings plus a content-aware tool gateway.
next_steps: Set enforcement.fail_closed_on_error on the Claude apps gateway and confirm that spend caps return 429 when Postgres is unavailable.
Route all inference through the configured AWS Gateway endpoint and test failover and per-model quotas.
Run denial tests against AWS Gateway for unknown tools and alternate egress paths, and allow only reviewed schemas and destinations.
Choose a content-aware MCP gateway for rate limits, schema validation and injection screening, and confirm Okta Agent Gateway GA status for the tenant.
unknowns: Which model providers and MCP servers the client actually uses, which decides whether the Claude apps gateway or AWS Gateway is the better fit.
Whether AWS Gateway screens prompts for injection, as the record does not say.
Whether Okta Agent Gateway is generally available for the client's tenant.
Whether any alternative content-aware MCP gateway or LLM gateway product is available, as no alternative records were supplied.
The client's deployed configurations, as none of the records tested a live tenant.

claims.text: Claude Code's self-hosted Claude apps gateway signs users in with the corporate IdP, enforces model access per IdP group, routes and fails over between Bedrock, Google Cloud, Foundry and the Anthropic API, and caps spend per user, group or organisation.

The Claude apps gateway has no documented prompt injection screening, spend enforcement fails open by default if Postgres is unavailable, and caps are USD estimates rather than token rate limits. Setting enforcement.fail_closed_on_error is the suggested fix.
AWS Gateway documents model-based routing across providers, but per-model quotas and failover semantics need verification on the selected route, and no deployed configuration was tested.

Claude Code enforces tool policy on the client side through permission rules, managed MCP allowlists, PreToolUse hooks and sandbox egress allowlists. This is not a separate gateway and has no tool quotas, rate limits or schema validation policy.
AWS Gateway exposes APIs and MCP tools with authentication, and policy checks tool calls. Unknown tools and alternate egress paths still need denial tests.

Okta Agent Gateway sits between agents and remote MCP servers, validates tokens, exposes only admin-selected tools and injects downstream credentials. It documents no rate limits, schema validation or injection screening, covers MCP only, and GA was stated for Q3.
Okta's gateway does not route, quota or screen model calls, so it does not serve as the model gateway.
Wiz has no model gateway. It checks that provider guardrails are enabled and flags AI endpoints not protected by Cloudflare, but enforcement at the edge is done by Cloudflare.
Purview offers only partial coverage. It has no model routing, quota or rate limits, and its prompt blocking is in preview.
Purview covers web search and AI site egress only, with no per-agent tool allow lists, schema checks or rate limits for tools.

concerns.concern: Can prompts, outputs and agent memory stay in Australia?
concerns.summary: The records do not confirm that prompts, outputs and agent memory can stay in Australia. Claude Code says residency follows the chosen provider or a gateway routing inference through the customer's cloud, and AWS residency needs service-specific validation. Purview does not address residency, and Wiz and Okta do not cover it.
next_steps: Confirm which inference provider and AWS Region Claude Code uses, and restrict it with allowedProviders and pinned model IDs in managed settings.
Trace each copy of prompts, outputs and memory in AgentCore and verify Region selection and deletion in the Australian Region.
Disable auto memory, feedback and nonessential traffic in Claude Code managed settings, and set cleanupPeriodDays.
Ask Microsoft for written confirmation of where Purview-retained AI interaction copies are stored.
unknowns: Whether the client's Claude Code deployment actually routes inference through an Australian Region.
Whether AgentCore Memory and Bedrock models are available in an Australian Region for the models chosen.
Where Anthropic stores cloud session transcripts and feedback transcripts geographically.
Where Purview retained AI interaction copies are stored.
Whether any of the in-stack controls have been tested, as all records are unverified.

claims.text: Claude Code residency follows the chosen provider, or a gateway that routes inference through the customer's cloud. Support is partial and unverified, so the required region has to be selected and confirmed.

Claude Code auto memory has no documented retention limit, and feedback transcripts are kept for 5 years when users submit them. Both are gaps for a residency position unless disabled in managed settings.
Claude Code auto memory is machine-local plaintext with no documented expiry. It can be disabled with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY where retention must be controlled.

Claude Code local session transcripts sit under the user's home directory and are retained for 30 days by default. Cloud session transcripts are stored by Anthropic, so location of that copy is not settled by these records.

Claude Code allows restricting API providers with allowedProviders and pinning model IDs on Bedrock, Google Cloud and Foundry. This can be used to keep inference on a chosen cloud, but organisation-level server-side model controls do not reach third-party cloud providers.
For AWS AgentCore memory, retention, downstream deletion and residency need service-specific validation. No Region or deployed configuration was tested, so Australian residency is not confirmed.
AWS Bedrock model, feature and Region availability must be checked for the selected deployment. The exact model identifier and supported Region should be recorded.
Purview retention policies can retain or delete prompts and responses, but residency is not addressed on the reviewed pages. Deletion can take up to about 16 days.
AWS AgentCore Memory persists events across sessions, which is the store where agent memory residency would need to be traced. Namespace access, correction and deletion should be tested.

concerns.concern: How do we make a person approve an agent action before it runs, with evidence of who approved it?
concerns.summary: Your stack can force a human approval before an agent action, but it only partly proves who approved it. Claude Code and Auth0 CIBA are the strongest routes, and each decision can be logged with a user identity, though neither is documented as tamper-evident. The audit capability you already have (c7-1) is partial, so approval evidence would need to be exported to write-once storage and tested.
next_steps: Set permissions.defaultMode or disableAutoMode in Claude Code managed settings so a human prompt is retained where approval is required.
Export Claude Code tool_decision events to write-once storage and confirm each carries the approving user's identity.
Pilot Auth0 CIBA with RAR for one high-risk agent action and test denial, expiry and replay behaviour.
Check with your Airia contact for the audit log schema and whether a receipt can be verified independently before considering it.
unknowns: Whether Purview offers any approval step for customer agents, as its record cites no source and only states none was found.
Whether your Claude Code deployment currently runs in Auto mode or Manual mode.
Whether your Auth0 plan includes CIBA.
How Auth0 CIBA handles binding message, expiry and replay.
Whether any in-stack log is tamper-evident, as none is documented as such.
Whether Airia can record a human approval event, as the record covers policy decisions only.

claims.text: Claude Code in Manual mode shows the exact command or edit and asks before running it. Unmatched commands fail closed to a prompt, and each decision is emitted as a tool_decision event with its source.

Claude Code gaps: Auto mode, the default in recent versions, replaces most human prompts with a classifier, and always-allow grants persist per repository. The approver is the local user with no separate authorisation check, so approval is not tied to a named authorised approver.

Auth0 for AI Agents offers CIBA with RAR, so an agent waits for a user to approve an action on a separate device with Guardian push showing the details. This is partial support, and CIBA needs an Auth0 Enterprise plan or add-on.
Okta workforce approval routing applies to access requests for agent-linked apps, not individual agent actions. Binding message, expiry and replay handling are not described on the page read.

Bedrock action groups support user confirmation and returning control to the application. Approval identity, expiry and replay protection need application tests, and no deployed configuration was tested.
Wiz has no approval step for actions an AI agent proposes. Its Workflows approval covers only Wiz's own containment actions, so it cannot supply this control.
Claude Code telemetry carries tool decisions with session and user attributes, which can serve as approval evidence. There is no tamper-evident ledger and local transcripts are editable by the user.

The Okta System Log records agent token exchanges and Agent Gateway logs every tool call. Tamper evidence, log schema and retention are not described on the pages read, and inputs and outputs are not captured.

Alternative if tamper-evident approval records are required: Airia release notes describe an AI Gateway feed with tamper-evident receipts covering identity, session, tool call, policy decision and outcome. The audit documentation requires a login and was not read, and human approval is not described.
